title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential, Shorten the Delay
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients may deteriorate with muted fever or inflammatory findings and have a broader pathogen differential. Severity, immune defect, exposure history and imaging pattern should drive urgent diagnostics and empiric therapy—not reassurance from a normal WBC or mild initial symptoms.
recognize: Risk depends on the immune defect: neutropenia, impaired cellular immunity, B-cell depletion, transplant and corticosteroid/biologic therapy create different infection patterns.
Common respiratory viruses can produce severe disease, while opportunistic fungal, mycobacterial or Pneumocystis infection may need consideration in the right host.
differentiate: Drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, malignancy and diffuse alveolar hemorrhage can mimic infection.
A normal chest x-ray early in severe immunocompromised-host infection does not reliably exclude lower-respiratory disease.
assessment: Define the immune defect, treatment timing/dose, neutrophil status, transplant history, prophylaxis, vaccination, travel/exposures and prior resistant organisms.
Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hemodynamics and subtle deterioration rather than waiting for classic inflammatory signs.
workup: Use prompt chest imaging and respiratory/microbiologic testing matched to severity and immune defect; CT or bronchoscopy may be needed when routine testing is nondiagnostic and risk remains high.
Obtain cultures before antimicrobials when feasible without delaying time-sensitive therapy in an unstable patient.
management: Escalate hypoxemia, hemodynamic instability, severe neutropenia with respiratory symptoms or rapidly progressive disease to acute specialty care.
Choose empiric antimicrobials according to immune defect, severity, prior microbiology and local guidance, then narrow when diagnostic evidence permits.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic function and major drug interactions matter with broad antimicrobials and transplant/immunosuppressive therapy.
Do not stop essential immunosuppression reflexively without coordinating the risk of rejection/disease flare against infection severity.
redFlags: Hemoptysis or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage concern
counselling: Teach early reporting of respiratory symptoms because immune suppression can blunt usual warning signs.
Maintain current vaccination/prevention plans appropriate to the immune condition.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/PCR/antigen studies and imaging; reassess quickly if outpatient management is selected for a carefully defined low-risk situation.
examTrap: Reassuring an immunocompromised patient with dyspnea because they are afebrile and the WBC is normal.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, absence of fever is weak reassurance—define the immune defect and act on physiology.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada respiratory-infection guidance for higher-risk/immunocompromised populations
